 What Really Happens If You Default on an SBA Loan (and Why It’s Not as Scary as You Think)
Hi Sara,
“I’ve got a 7(a) loan… what happens if I default?”
It’s the question everyone wants to ask—but no one actually asks their banker. And honestly, I get it. Walking into a loan meeting and saying, “Hey, what happens if this all goes sideways?” isn’t exactly confidence-inspiring.
So I asked for you.
Recently, I sat down with Eric Rabinovich from Live Oak Bank—an SBA lender who actually knows his stuff. And we dug into the unspoken anxiety a lot of small business buyers carry: what if I can’t make my payments?
Here’s what you should know (but probably won’t hear from your loan officer):
Default isn’t common. SBA 7(a) loans are underwritten carefully, especially in industries like professional services. So before you panic, know that defaults are rare—and you’re likely not alone if you’re just feeling nervous rather than actually in trouble.

There is a big difference between “I’m anxious” and “I’m about to miss a payment.” If it’s the latter—call the bank. Early. Not calling won’t help, and lenders often have options like maturity extensions or forbearance tools they may be willing to explore—especially before you miss a payment.

If you’re within the first 18 months? The stakes may be higher. A default in that window can trigger an audit of the loan by the SBA, and if the bank didn’t follow the SOPs to a tee, they could lose the government guarantee. So yes—they might feel extra motivated to work something out early on.

The “personal guarantee” isn’t just a scary phrase. If you do default, banks aren’t always trying to squeeze value from your business (especially if it’s mostly goodwill and a copier on lease). Instead, they go for your personal assets. Yes, that includes your house if it's tied to the loan—and exemptions vary wildly by state. (California’s, for instance, is laughably low.)

Bottom line?
Don’t stick your head in the sand. If you’re feeling the squeeze, talk to your lender. If you’re about to close and just realized your second home could become part of the SBA’s repo wish list… definitely know what you’re signing.
And if you’re doing a smaller deal (under $500K)? Live Oak has a killer Express Loan product that’s actually made for your world.

Sara Sharp
